name: Andrea del Sarto
teaser: The Florentine painter Vasari called 'the flawless painter' — technically perfect, self-consciously so, which is why Raphael reportedly said his figures lacked 'loftiness.' He was the teacher of Pontormo and Rosso, and his Madonnas are serene beyond belief.

exploreAction.targetName: Madonna of the Harpies (Uffizi, Florence) — the pedestal
exploreAction.instruction: Mary stands on a pedestal carved with harpies — the emblem of a plague hospital where the painting hung. Look at the perfect symmetry, the studied calm, the color harmony. Del Sarto's tragedy is that he's so good at everything that nothing startles.

name: Rosso Fiorentino
teaser: The restless Florentine who invented Mannerism with Pontormo — elongated bodies, sour colors, and emotions turned up past the breaking point. He later fled to France and founded the School of Fontainebleau, decorating the king's palace in a style that shocked polite taste.

exploreAction.instruction: The Deposition in Volterra is Mannerism in a bottle: anguished faces, frozen ladders, and a palette of acid pinks and greens. Look at the two thieves still on their crosses — one of them looks straight at you. Nothing here is calm or 'correct,' and that's the point.

name: Jacopo Pontormo
teaser: The most neurotic genius of Florentine Mannerism — a reclusive painter whose figures twist like flames and whose colors glow unearthly pink. His Deposition in the Capponi Chapel is one of the strangest, most beautiful paintings of the 1520s.

exploreAction.targetName: The Deposition (Capponi Chapel, Florence) — the colors
exploreAction.instruction: No cross, no tomb, no ground — just figures in a pink-and-mint cloud, floating in grief. Look at the colors: watermelon pinks, pale blues, acid green — decades before their time. Pontormo kept a secret diary full of his terrors; this painting is the visible part.

name: Giorgione
teaser: The mysterious Venetian who died at 32 and changed painting forever — credited with making landscape and mood, not story, the subject of art. The Tempest, his most famous work, has never been decoded and maybe isn't meant to be.

exploreAction.instruction: A soldier, a nude woman nursing a baby, and a lightning bolt over a city. No one knows the story — the painter gave it no title. Look at the weather: the storm is the real subject. Giorgione invented the painting that means whatever you feel it means.

name: Fra Bartolomeo
teaser: The Dominican friar-painter of Florence who burned his secular drawings after joining Savonarola's movement, then rebuilt his art on serenity — his balanced, glowing altarpieces influenced Raphael and earned him the nickname 'Fra Bartolomeo of the beautiful colors.'

exploreAction.targetName: The Mystic Marriage of St. Catherine (Louvre) — the balance
exploreAction.instruction: A perfectly symmetrical composition: Mary and the saints arranged like a bell curve of holiness. Look at how the drapery falls in heavy, majestic folds and how the light is even, calm, and warm. Fra Bartolomeo painted faith as a state of rest.

name: Antonio Allegri da Correggio
teaser: The Parma painter who invented the ceiling as a hole in the sky — his Assumption of the Virgin is a swirling vortex of saints and clouds seen from below, a century before Baroque illusionism. His figures are soft, sweet, and impossibly foreshortened.

exploreAction.targetName: The Assumption of the Virgin (Parma Cathedral dome) — look up
exploreAction.instruction: Lie back or tilt your head: the dome is open to heaven, crowded with swirling bodies and cloud banks painted from below (sotto in sù). Correggio even painted the viewer's shadow in — a leg dangling over the edge of the frame. This dome invented the Baroque ceiling.

name: Parmigianino
teaser: The Mannerist who stretched elegance to the breaking point — his Madonna with the Long Neck turns anatomy into a swan song. He was also a self-portraitist who painted his face in a convex mirror at 21, his hand bulging like a fisheye lens.

exploreAction.targetName: The Madonna with the Long Neck (Uffizi, Florence) — the neck
exploreAction.instruction: Mary's neck curves like a column of ivory, the Christ child's fingers and the angels' legs stretch impossibly long, and in the background a tiny figure unrolls a scroll with no message. It's elegance gone hallucinatory — the definition of Mannerism.

name: Annibale Carracci
teaser: The Bolognese painter who rebooted art after Mannerism — his ceiling of the Farnese Gallery is a full-blown classical universe of gods and heroes that became the bible of Baroque. He also invented caricature as a genre.

exploreAction.targetName: The Farnese Gallery ceiling (Rome) — the frames
exploreAction.instruction: Stand in the middle of the gallery and look up: scenes from mythology are stacked inside fake frames and false bronze medallions, a museum in the sky. Notice the famous 'Polyphemus' and the corner figures that climb over the frame. Carracci made painting theatrical.

name: Guido Reni
teaser: The Bolognese painter of heavenly sweetness — his Aurora, Dawn, and weeping Magdalens were so beloved that for two centuries he was considered the greatest painter alive. His Salome with the head of John the Baptist is quietly chilling.

exploreAction.instruction: Apollo drives his chariot across a dawn sky, surrounded by dancing Hours. Look at the pale, luminous light and the idealized faces — Reni smoothed out all grit. His style was so seductive that critics later rebelled against it; first love him, then judge him.

name: Carlo Crivelli
teaser: The Gothic-surreal Venetian who decorated his Madonnas with cucumbers, flies, and glowing marble — a painter who combined Byzantine gold, Renaissance perspective, and a delicious weirdness. His fruits and insects are more famous than his saints.

exploreAction.targetName: The Annunciation with Saint Emidius (National Gallery, London) — the cucumber
exploreAction.instruction: Look past the golden architecture to the props: a cucumber, a fly, a peacock — symbols of sin, corruption, and immortality, painted with obsessive precision. Crivelli loved the odd detail. Notice how the angel and Mary are separated by a street of impossible perspective.

name: Pietro Perugino
teaser: The Umbrian master who taught Raphael and perfected the sweet, spacious devotional scene — his Deliverance of the Keys is a lesson in perspective and calm. His figures stand in infinite landscapes, gently aware of God.

exploreAction.targetName: The Delivery of the Keys (Sistine Chapel, Vatican) — the space
exploreAction.instruction: Christ hands the keys to Peter in the foreground while a perfect plaza, a temple, and an arch recede behind them in flawless one-point perspective. Look at the crowd: every face is placid, every gesture dignified. Perugino painted heaven as a tidy, sunlit town.

name: Bernardo Daddi
teaser: The 14th-century Florentine who brought tenderness into Gothic altarpieces — his small panels of the Virgin are intimate, human, and richly detailed, a bridge between Byzantine icons and the humanism of the coming Renaissance.

exploreAction.targetName: The Madonna and Child with Saints (various) — the intimacy
exploreAction.instruction: Look at how Daddi's Mary leans toward her child, how the saints share quiet glances — a warmth almost unknown in earlier icons. His gold backgrounds are luminous, his tiny narrative panels tell whole stories in inches. Gothic art becoming human.

name: Duccio di Buoninsegna
teaser: The Sienese master whose Maestà — a towering altarpiece painted on both sides — turned Byzantine stiffness into lyricism. When it was carried through Siena in 1311, the whole city shut down to celebrate; it's now considered the hinge of Italian painting.

exploreAction.targetName: The Maestà (Museo dell'Opera del Duomo, Siena) — the details
exploreAction.instruction: The front shows the Madonna enthroned among angels and saints; the back is a 40-scene story of Christ. Look at the small panels — the Entry into Jerusalem, the Betrayal — where Duccio compresses narrative, architecture, and feeling into inches of gold.

name: Simone Martini
teaser: The Sienese Gothic master of elegance — his Annunciation in the Uffizi, with its gilded wings, swaying Virgin, and Latin protest from Gabriel, is one of the most refined paintings of the Middle Ages. Petrarch owned one of his portraits and wrote poems to it.

exploreAction.instruction: Gabriel's wings are gold leaf and his greeting is literally written in the air; Mary recoils so hard her cloak flies. Look at the inscription — she asks how this can be — and the response carved along the frame. Simone painted the most polite, most luxurious shock in art.

name: Ambrogio Lorenzetti
teaser: The Sienese painter who painted politics — his fresco cycle of Good and Bad Government in Siena's town hall is the first great secular painting in Western art, a vast panorama of a city and its countryside flourishing under justice, or collapsing under tyranny.

exploreAction.targetName: Allegory of Good Government (Palazzo Pubblico, Siena) — the city
exploreAction.instruction: On one wall, a city of towers, markets, dancers, and builders under the benign figure of Good Government; on the opposite wall, the same city in rubble under Tyranny. Look at the details — the hanging body, the broken gates, the fear in the faces. Political art, 1338.

name: Masaccio
teaser: The Florentine who died at 26 and invented Renaissance painting — his Expulsion from Eden is the first nude since antiquity that feels like a real body in real space, and his Tribute Money fresco gave painting depth, weight, and shadow.

exploreAction.targetName: The Expulsion from Eden (Brancacci Chapel, Florence) — the grief
exploreAction.instruction: Adam covers his face, Eve covers her body, both scream silently as an angel drives them out. Look at their feet — solid, shadowed, standing on real ground. Masaccio's light comes from a single source, like a stage. This fresco taught the next 500 years how to paint.

name: Domenico Veneziano
teaser: The mysterious Venetian who brought oil and light to Florence — his St. Lucy Altarpiece is a breakthrough in pale, glowing color and architectural space. Almost nothing is known of his life; he may have been poisoned by a jealous rival.

exploreAction.targetName: St. Lucy Altarpiece (Uffizi, Florence) — the colors
exploreAction.instruction: A pink-robed Virgin sits in a painted porch, her face lit by morning light. Look at the pale colors — the whites, the rose, the pale blue — decades ahead of his time. Veneziano's palette is so light it makes other Florentines look heavy. A breakthrough in color, and a mystery of a life.

name: Paolo Uccello
teaser: The Florentine who fell in love with perspective — his three panels of the Battle of San Romano scatter lances, horses, and helmets across a tilted chessboard of a battlefield. His wife reportedly called him to bed and he'd answer: 'What a sweet thing perspective is!'

exploreAction.targetName: The Battle of San Romano (National Gallery, London) — the lances
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the fallen lances: each one is a perspective line lying flat on the ground, pointing toward a vanishing point. The horses rear in impossible poses, the armor glints like metal toys. Uccello turned a battle into a geometry lesson and somehow made it glorious.

name: Antonello da Messina
teaser: The Sicilian who brought Flemish oil technique to Italy — his portraits stare out with a psychological presence no one in Italy had painted before. St. Jerome in His Study packs an entire world into a single arched frame.

exploreAction.targetName: St. Jerome in His Study (National Gallery, London) — the architecture
exploreAction.instruction: Inside one Gothic arch: a church interior, a scholar's desk, books, a lion, a cardinal's hat, and a landscape through the windows — all painted with Flemish microscopic detail. Look at the light through the leaded glass, the shadow on the books. Everything in focus, everything alive.
